chapters.title: Same video, two titles
beats: Maya posts a video of her favorite weeknight pasta.
She calls it: My Pasta Recipe.
A week later, it has barely moved.
So she changes one thing. Not the video. Not the thumbnail. Just the title.
Because a title is often the reason someone gives your video a chance, or scrolls right past it.
The new one says: The Ten Minute Pasta I Make Every Week.
Same video, same thumbnail. And more people start clicking.
In this video, you'll learn how to write titles like that, step by step, with formulas you can use today.

chapters.title: What a title is for
beats: First, what is a title actually for?
When someone sees your video, they see two things: a thumbnail, and a title.
The thumbnail grabs their eye. The title tells them why this video is worth their time.
Think of it as a promise. If you click, here's what you'll get.
Click, and you'll learn something. Click, and you'll laugh. Click, and you'll see how the story ends.
A great title makes that promise clear, makes it interesting, and then the video keeps it.
Keep that word in mind: promise. Everything in this video comes back to it.

chapters.title: Put the best words first
beats: Rule number one: put the best words first.
On a phone, long titles often get cut off after about fifty or sixty characters.
So if your title starts slow, the good part might never be seen.
Look at this one: In today's video I'm going to show you how I make pasta in ten minutes.
On a small screen, people only read: In today's video I'm going to show you.
Flip it around. Ten Minute Pasta. Now the most interesting words land first.
A simple target: aim for under sixty characters, and make the first few words do the heavy lifting.

chapters.title: Be specific
beats: Vague titles are easy to scroll past, because they could be about anything.
Easy Dinner Ideas could be any video on YouTube.
Three Dinners Under Five Dollars is a picture in your head.
Numbers help. Times, prices, amounts, days.
Ten minutes is more believable than fast. Five dollars is more believable than cheap.
Results help too. Not, how I cook, but, how I cook a week of meals in one hour.
The more exact the promise, the easier it is to believe, and the easier it is to want.

chapters.title: Make it about the viewer
beats: Rule three: make it about the viewer, not about you.
My Trip to Rome is about you. Unless people already know you, it's hard to care.
How to See Rome in One Day, on a Budget, is about them.
Ask yourself: who is this for, and what do they get?
Maya used to write: My new sourdough attempt.
Now she writes: Your First Sourdough, the Easy Way.
Same bread. But now the viewer can see themselves in the title.

chapters.title: Open a loop
beats: People click when there's a small gap between what they know and what they want to know.
I Tried Cooking Without Oil for Thirty Days. What happened?
The Mistake That Ruins Most Homemade Pizza. Which mistake? Am I making it?
That little itch is curiosity, and it's one of the strongest reasons to click.
But here's the rule: always close the loop. Give the answer in the video, and don't make people wait forever for it.
A loop you never close isn't curiosity. It's a trick, and viewers remember tricks.

chapters.title: Words with feeling
beats: Rule five: pick words with feeling.
Some words carry emotion on their own. Easy. Mistake. Finally. Never. Secret. Surprising.
Compare: Tips for Better Rice, with: Stop Making This Rice Mistake.
The second one feels urgent. It speaks to a worry the viewer already has.
Use these words like salt. A little brings out the flavor. Too much, and nobody trusts it.
And skip the all caps titles. One word in capitals can add punch. A whole title in capitals just looks like shouting.

chapters.title: Search or browse
beats: Now, people find videos in two main ways, and each one wants a slightly different title.
Search is when someone types a question. How to fix runny scrambled eggs.
For search, use the words people actually type. Plain and clear beats clever.
Here's a free trick: start typing your topic into the YouTube search bar, and look at the suggestions. Those are real searches.
If you see how to make fluffy pancakes, and your video shows exactly that, you have your title's first words.
Browse is the home page and suggested videos. Nobody asked for your video. It has to catch their interest on its own.
For browse, lean on curiosity, feeling and specific results.
The best titles often do both: a searchable phrase, with a little spark.

chapters.title: Title and thumbnail, one team
beats: Your title never works alone. It sits right next to your thumbnail.
So don't make them say the same thing.
If the thumbnail already says Ten Minute Pasta, a title that also says Ten Minute Pasta wastes the space.
Let the thumbnail show, and let the title tell.
The thumbnail shows the finished pasta and a timer. The title adds the part a picture can't: The Pasta I Make Every Week, In Ten Minutes.
Together they tell one story. And if you missed it, the thumbnails video in this series goes deeper on that half.

chapters.title: Five title formulas
beats: Here are five formulas you can steal.
One. How to get a result, without the pain. How to Make Bread Without Kneading.
Two. I tried something, for a set time. I Cooked Only From My Freezer for a Week.
Three. A number, and the mistakes. Five Mistakes That Make Your Cookies Flat.
Four. Why something surprising is true. Why Restaurant Rice Tastes Better Than Yours.
Five. This versus that. Cheap Pan Versus Expensive Pan.
Formulas aren't cheating. They're a starting shape. You fill them with your own topic and your own words.

chapters.title: Write ten, pick one
beats: The best way to find a great title? Write a lot of bad ones first.
Maya writes ten titles for every video. Fast, no judging.
Then she crosses out the boring ones, the long ones, and the ones that promise too much.
She reads the last two out loud, and asks: which one would I click?
Out loud is the secret. If it sounds clumsy when you say it, it'll read clumsy too.
After posting, she checks YouTube Studio. It shows how often people click when they see the video. That's called click through rate.
If a video gets seen but not clicked, she tries a new title. You can change a title any time, it doesn't hurt the video.

chapters.title: Mistakes to avoid
beats: Promising something the video doesn't deliver. People click, feel tricked, and leave fast. And YouTube notices when viewers leave.
Stuffing in keywords. Pasta Recipe, Easy Pasta, Best Pasta, Pasta Twenty Twenty Six. That reads like a robot wrote it.
Inside jokes. A title that only makes sense if you've seen the video won't make anyone click it.
And copying the exact title of a big channel. You'll just look like the smaller version of them.
Your channel is yours. Let your titles sound like you.

chapters.title: Your title checklist
beats: So, a month later, Maya looks back at her channel.
The videos are the same quality as before. But now the titles tell people exactly why to watch, and more of them do.
Here's your checklist. Best words first. Be specific. Make it about the viewer. Open a loop, and close it. Use words with feeling, but not too many.
And every title is a promise. Write one you can keep.
Next time you upload, write ten titles before you pick one. Then come back and tell me which one won.
It feels slow at first. After a few videos, it takes five minutes, and it becomes the most valuable five minutes of your upload.
And if you want your thumbnails to match, watch How to Make Thumbnails People Click next. See you there.
